sources.lshk-1997: Linguistic Society of Hong Kong (1997). 粵語拼音字表 (Guide to LSHK Cantonese Romanization of Chinese Characters). The Jyutping scheme.

teach.text: Cantonese has six tones. The pitch of a syllable is part of the word, so si1 and si6 are different words.

Pitch is written with Chao numbers, from 1 (lowest) to 5 (highest): tone 1 high level 55 (53), tone 2 high rising 35, tone 3 mid level 33, tone 4 low falling 21 (11), tone 5 low rising 23, tone 6 low level 22.
The numbers in brackets are normal variants: tone 1 is also said as a high fall (53), and tone 4 is often heard as low level (11).
Jyutping writes the tone as a digit after the syllable: 詩 si1, 史 si2, 試 si3, 時 si4, 市 si5, 事 si6, and 分 fan1, 粉 fan2, 訓 fan3, 墳 fan4, 奮 fan5, 份 fan6.
Tones 1, 3 and 6 are level and differ only in height: tone 1 is high (55), tone 3 mid (33), tone 6 low (22).
Tones 2 and 5 both rise: tone 2 rises high (35), tone 5 rises only a little from low (23).
Tones 4 and 6 are both low: tone 4 falls to the bottom (21), tone 6 stays level (22).
Syllables ending in -p, -t or -k are short: the stop at the end cuts the vowel off. They use only three pitches: high, mid and low.
Traditional accounts count these short syllables as three extra tones, which is why Cantonese is often said to have nine tones. In pitch they match tones 1, 3 and 6.
So Jyutping numbers them 1, 3 and 6: 色 sik1, 錫 sek3, 食 sik6.
Jyutping has 19 initial consonants: b p m f d t n l g k ng h gw kw w z c s j. A syllable can also begin with a vowel.
b, d, g are unaspirated and voiceless: Jyutping b sounds like an unaspirated English "p", as in "spin". p, t, k are aspirated, with a puff of air, as in "pin".
The same contrast runs through gw/kw (g and k with rounded lips) and z/c (an unaspirated and an aspirated "ts").
ng can begin a syllable, like the "ng" of English "sing". Many speakers drop it, so ngo5 is often heard as o5.
aa is long and a is short: 三 saam1 has a long vowel, 心 sam1 a short one.
yu, oe and eo are said with rounded lips: yu is "ee" with rounded lips, oe is the "e" of "bed" with rounded lips, and eo is a short rounded vowel that comes only in eoi, eon and eot.
The nasal endings -m, -n and -ng keep words apart: sam1, san1 and sang1 are different syllables.
The stop endings -p, -t and -k are unreleased: the lips or tongue close and hold, with no puff of air after.
m and ng can be whole syllables: 唔 m4 (not) and 五 ng5 (five). There are no recordings of these two in the app yet.
Jyutping is the romanisation of the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong. A syllable is written initial + final + tone digit: s + ik + 6 = sik6.
Some letters differ from English: j is the "y" of "yes" (ji1), z and c are "ts" sounds, and yu, oe and eo are rounded vowels.
A tone is a pitch shape within your own voice: high level 55, high rising 35, mid level 33, low falling 21, low rising 23, low level 22. Match the shape, not the recording's exact pitch.
